chapter_theme: Kovalan, at dawn, leaves Kannaki in Kavunthi's keeping, and the nun answers his self-reproach with a teaching that the deed ripens on its doer and that suffering comes to those bound to women, citing two exiled kings who lost their wives, and assures him that he, unlike them, keeps his wife; he then walks through Madurai's courtesans' quarter through all its seasons, its dancers' streets, bazaar, gem, gold, cloth and grain streets, and goes back outside the walls pleased with the city that will kill him.

cast.role: the merchant's son of Puhar, Kannaki's husband
the woman ascetic who guides Kovalan and Kannaki to Madurai

silappathikaram:14:1-14.reading: At dawn, as birds rise crying from the groves, pools and fields and the sun opens the lotus, Madurai of the sword-bearing Seliyan wakes, and in the temples of the three-eyed god, of the one who raised the eagle banner, of the white one with the plough banner and of the one with the cock banner, in the monasteries of the righteous and in the king's palace the morning drums sound with the conch.
silappathikaram:14:1-14.nuance: The list sets the shrines of four gods and the பள்ளி of the அறவோர் (the renouncers' monasteries) beside the palace, the seat of மறம், as one waking city: line 11's அறத்துறை and line 12's மறத்துறை are paired, and Kavunthi will use the same two words a few lines on (27-28) for the paths of harm and of virtue. The sun is called the orb the world worships that makes kings tremble (line 5), a mild foretaste in a kaathai that ends at this king's city.
silappathikaram:14:1-14.event: Dawn breaks over Madurai and the morning drums sound in its temples, monasteries and palace.
silappathikaram:14:1-14.unit_note: Moved the end of the first unit from line 12 to line 14: the list of temples in lines 7-12 is the subject of இயம்ப in line 14, which closes the sentence of the dawn.

silappathikaram:14:15-24.reading: Kovalan goes to Kavunthi, who keeps to her vows, worships her and says that, having become like those who strayed from the right path, he has brought distress on his tender wife and suffered among strangers in an unknown land, and asks whether, until he has made his state known to the merchants of the old city and returned, any harm could come to her here in the lady's keeping.
silappathikaram:14:15-24.nuance: Kovalan names his own fault (நெறியின் நீங்கியோர் நீர்மையேன், line 17) before Kavunthi names karma (line 27): the two causes, his choice and the ripening deed, are set side by side within a few lines, and the nun's answer moves the weight from the first to the second. மன்னர் பின்னோர் (line 21), 'those after the kings', is read here as the merchant order, to whom Kovalan as a merchant's son would go.
silappathikaram:14:15-24.event: Kovalan asks Kavunthi to keep Kannaki safe while he goes into Madurai to make himself known to its merchants.
silappathikaram:14:15-24.unit_note: Moved the start from line 13 to line 15 and the end from line 29 to line 24: Kovalan's speech runs from line 15 to என்றலும் in line 24, and Kavunthi's answer begins at line 25.

silappathikaram:14:25-49.reading: Kavunthi tells Kovalan that the unlearned do not take the drum-like cry of the righteous to leave the ways of harm because the hard deed will feed its fruit, and are bewildered when that deed ripens, while the learned do not despair when they eat the fruit of their deeds; that the pains of parting, of union and of the bodiless god's punishment belong to those who join with women and not to the strong who live alone; that those who took women and food for pleasure have met grief ever since; and that he surely knows the old story of the one who went with his wife at his father's word and suffered when she was taken from him.
silappathikaram:14:25-49.nuance: Kavunthi's word for the deed's coming, உருத்த (line 31), is the verb of the patikam's third moral (ஊழ்வினை உருத்துவந்து ஊட்டும்): the epic's thesis is first spoken inside the story here, by a nun consoling the man it will kill. She names neither hero of her exempla: the one 'who begot the first of the Veda' (line 48) is the god who fathered Brahma, here in his birth as the prince exiled with his wife, and the reader must supply the name. Her account of desire as the root of suffering is a renouncer's, yet she does not urge Kovalan to leave his wife; the speech consoles a householder with an ascetic's diagnosis. தவந்தீர் மருங்கின் (line 26) may mean that his lone suffering comes from a lack of past penance; the reading does not turn on it. The unit does not name a school; the speaker is the Jain nun of the earlier kaathais.
silappathikaram:14:25-49.event: Kavunthi answers Kovalan with a teaching on karma and on the suffering that comes through desire, citing the prince who lost his wife in exile.

claims.claim: a hard deed brings its fruit back on the doer, so one should leave the ways of harm
the learned do not despair when they eat the fruit of their deeds, while the unlearned are bewildered by it
the pains of parting, union and desire belong to those joined with women, not to the strong who live alone
those who hold women and food to be pleasure meet a suffering they did not reckon on

silappathikaram:14:25-49.unit_note: Moved the start from line 30 to line 25: Kavunthi's speech begins at கவுந்தி கூறும் (line 25), and lines 25-29 begin the sentence that ends at கொள்ளார் (line 30). The end stays at line 49 (நெடுமொழி யன்றோ).

silappathikaram:14:50-61.reading: Kavunthi adds the example of the king who lost his land at the dice and went into the cruel forest with his wife, not parted from her for want of love nor she guilty of any fault, and asks whether his leaving her in the forest at midnight was not strong karma, and whether Kovalan would not say so if anyone blamed the woman; Kovalan, she says, is not even like him, for he has a life never parted from his wife, so let him go without grief, learn a fitting place in the king's Koodal and come back.
silappathikaram:14:50-61.nuance: The nun's comfort is that Kovalan, unlike the dice-ruined king, keeps his wife at his side (பிரியா வாழ்க்கை, line 59); the story will part them within days, and Kannaki will name the same driving deed (ஊழ்வினை) in the Pandya's court. The exemplum clears the abandoned wife of blame and lays the abandonment on karma rather than on the husband's will. Line 57 (சொல்லலும் உண்டேற் சொல்லா யோநீ) is compressed; it is read here as an appeal to Kovalan to answer anyone who blames the wife.
silappathikaram:14:50-61.event: Kavunthi cites the dice-ruined king who abandoned his wife in the forest and sends Kovalan into Madurai to find a lodging.

claims.claim: a husband's abandonment of his innocent wife was the work of strong karma, not her fault

silappathikaram:14:50-61.unit_note: Moved the end from line 59 to line 61: Kavunthi's speech closes with போதீங் கென்றலும் (line 61), so lines 60-61 belong to it rather than to the entry into the city.

silappathikaram:14:62-76.reading: Kovalan goes along the tunnel road beside the moat where elephant herds pass, enters the guarded gate unsuspected by its Yavana swordsmen, and comes into the walled city that opens like Indra's jewel casket, with banners waving in the west wind, where courtesans with their lovers play in the Vaigai's flood at the marutham-shaded ford and wear mullai, kuvalai and other flowers.
silappathikaram:14:62-76.nuance: The Yavana guards at the gate are a detail of the city's wealth and order; that they do not question the stranger is the first of the many ways the city lets Kovalan in without knowing him.
silappathikaram:14:62-76.unit_note: Moved the start from line 60 to line 62: lines 60-61 close Kavunthi's speech (என்றலும், line 61), and Kovalan's walk into the city begins at line 62.
silappathikaram:14:62-76.event: Kovalan enters Madurai through its guarded gate and begins his walk through its streets.

silappathikaram:14:77-101.reading: The courtesans, garlanded with lilies, jasmine and red waterlily and wearing Korkai pearls, smear Malaya sandal and play in the groves, sit at evening on moonlit terraces in red silk with hill flowers, saffron and coral to show Indra the red adornment of Koodal, and, besides the season when the cloud-king comes with the north wind, warm themselves by agil fires with their men and close the small windows in the cold.
silappathikaram:14:77-101.nuance: The description runs through the seasons in a single sentence (lines 70-145): each season is a new setting for the same pleasures of the courtesans' quarter, and their dress follows the seasons' colours. Which season each sub-scene names is not always clear from the Tamil, and the reading keeps to what the lines show.

silappathikaram:14:102-111.reading: In the early dew season, when the sun has gone south and white clouds rarely show, the men and women of rich houses enjoy the young sun on moonlit terraces, and besides that the east wind comes in bearing the agil, silk, sandal, scents and camphor that the people of Thondi have loaded on their ships.

silappathikaram:14:112-127.reading: Wondering where the king of dew has gone at the union of Panguni and where the young spring is, which comes with the south wind from Pothiyil when the madhavi creeper lifts its banner, the women count the seasons with their husbands; and when the summer king who ruled Koodal with forest fires departs on the last day of fierce heat, carriages, palanquins and jewelled couches are given them.
silappathikaram:14:112-127.nuance: Line 113's கோதை மாதவி is the madhavi creeper whose flowering marks spring, but in an epic whose Madhavi is the courtesan Kovalan left, the creeper raising its banner over a courtesans' quarter is hard to read without her.

silappathikaram:14:128-145.reading: Given chowries, gold betel-pouches and sharp swords by the prince, the women of unfailing wealth take new lovers, drink the toddy their maids bear in gold bowls, and in their sulks show the unspoken laugh, the fight of the eye's corner, the curled brow and the sweat on the small forehead, in the street where rich men who wait on their moods and the kings of the earth take delight.
silappathikaram:14:128-145.unit_note: Moved the end from line 143 to line 145: the list of the women's sulking signs closes with வீதியும் (line 145), which ends the description of this street.

silappathikaram:14:146-167.reading: There are also the two great streets of those of the sixty-four arts, whose sweet words outdo song: the houses of flawless fame before which crowned kings bow, where women who know the two styles of dance, its measures, the vari, songs and beats and the instruments, the four kinds of gesture and the stage of seven levels, the talaikkol dancer, the singer of the vaaram and the dancers of the lead and middle songs, receive the thousand and eight kalanju by fixed rule each day, and in the net of whose glances even ascetics lose their hard-won wisdom, while young men and the fools of love's feast sleep secure.
silappathikaram:14:146-167.nuance: The fee, ஆயிரத் தெண்கழஞ்சு with எட்டுக் கடைநிறுத்த, and the praise வடுநீங்கு சிறப்பின் are the words used when Madhavi received her title and price in Puhar; here they describe a daily rate across a whole profession. சுடுமண் ஏறா (line 146) is obscure and the reading leaves it aside; தாக்கணங்கு (line 160) is the goddess who strikes those who look on her.
silappathikaram:14:146-167.unit_note: Moved the start from line 144 to line 146 and the end from line 156 to line 167: the dancers' quarter begins at line 146 and its sentence ends at இருபெரு வீதியும் (line 167).

silappathikaram:14:168-179.reading: There is the bazaar street, desired by kings for its wealth, where carriages, chariot parts, armour, goads, leather shields, chowries and shields of boar-hide and of wood lie heaped with work in copper and bronze, things of silk and garlands, polished wares, worked horn and ivory, incense, sandal and flowers, so mixed in plenty that their kinds cannot be told apart.
silappathikaram:14:168-179.unit_note: Moved the start from line 157 to line 168 and the end from line 172 to line 179: the list of the bazaar's goods begins at line 168 and ends with அங்காடி வீதியும் (line 179).

silappathikaram:14:180-200.reading: There is the gem street, safe from any enemy, where men who can tell gems apart gather: diamonds free of the four flaws the treatises name, in the colours of the four orders, emeralds free of dark spots, rubies of every lawful kind, topaz, crystal and stones dark or of two colours, gems whose flaws from wind, earth, stone or water have been cut away, pearls round as the moon, Jupiter and Mars, and coral without twist.
silappathikaram:14:180-200.nuance: Each gem is named with the flaws it lacks, so the street is a street of judgment as much as of wealth: its people know by rule what is true and what is false in a stone. The epic will bring a gem-filled anklet before this king, and his verdict will be made without any such testing.
silappathikaram:14:180-200.unit_note: Moved the start from line 173 to line 180 and the end from line 195 to line 200: the gems begin at line 180 and the sentence closes at வீதியும் (line 200).

silappathikaram:14:201-218.reading: Past the gold street, where assayers of the four kinds of gold raise their flags free of doubt, the cloth street of cotton, hair and silk in bundles past counting, and the grain street where weighers, measurers and those with the measuring pot go everywhere among heaped grain and sacks of pepper, Kovalan wanders the four-caste streets, junctions, squares, halls and lanes, and, glad at having seen the king's great city under the shade of banners the sun cannot pierce, goes back outside the walls.
silappathikaram:14:201-218.nuance: பொலந்தெரி மாக்கள் (line 203), the men who test gold, are the trade of the goldsmith who will accuse Kovalan; the tour ends in pleasure (மகிழ்வெய்தி) at the city whose verdict will kill him.
silappathikaram:14:201-218.event: Kovalan walks through the gold, cloth and grain streets and, pleased with the city, returns outside its walls.
silappathikaram:14:201-218.unit_note: Moved the start from line 196 to line 201: line 200 closes the gem street, and line 201 opens the gold street.

links.note: The patikam announces as the epic's third moral that the deed of former birth comes in wrath and feeds its fruit (ஊழ்வினை உருத்துவந்து ஊட்டும்); Kavunthi says the hard deed feeds its fruit and that the unlearned are bewildered when the evil deed comes in wrath (உருத்த காலை).
links.teaches: The moral Ilango states from outside the story is first spoken inside it by a nun who uses it to console Kovalan for a hardship already past, so the reader hears the thesis as comfort just before it becomes the account of his death.

links.note: Kavunthi assures Kovalan that, unlike the dice-ruined king who left his wife in the forest by strong karma, he has a life never parted from his wife; in the Pandya's court Kannaki says her husband came to Madurai driven by ஊழ்வினை and was killed.
links.teaches: The nun's karma, invoked to show that Kovalan's lot is better than the exiled king's, is the same force Kannaki names when she stands parted from him for ever, so the consolation becomes the epic's irony: the karma Kavunthi uses to excuse a parting is already moving toward a worse one.

links.note: The couplet asks why those who take good fortune as good grieve when ill fortune comes; Kavunthi says the learned do not despair when they eat the fruit of their deeds, while the unlearned are bewildered when the evil deed ripens.
links.teaches: The couplet's argument for calm rests on consistency between good and bad fortune, while the nun rests it on learning and adds a cause, desire for women and food, so the pair shows the Kural's equanimity before fate being turned into a renouncer's diagnosis of where suffering comes from.

gains.a: Kavunthi's counsel gains a compact general rule behind it, so her talk of the learned not despairing reads as a recognised teaching rather than private comfort
gains.b: the couplet gains a hearer and an occasion, a ruined husband in a strange city, and a second argument for calm that it does not make, that the suffering was earned by desire

links.note: The quatrain says that because a wife cannot be put away even if she lacks virtue and bears no child, the learned called marriage கடி; Kavunthi says the pains of parting and union belong only to those joined with women, not to the strong who live alone.
links.teaches: Both make marriage a source of suffering from which the solitary are free, but the Naladiyar argues it to recommend renunciation while Kavunthi states it to a married man and then sends him on with his wife, so the pair shows the renouncer's diagnosis offered without its prescription.

gains.a: the nun's claim gains the ethical tradition's own argument for why the bond brings pain, that it cannot be undone
gains.b: the quatrain gains a case where its view is spoken to a husband who is not told to leave his wife, which limits how far the ascetic diagnosis is meant to bind a householder

links.note: In Puhar Madhavi received by the king's rule the thousand and eight kalanju (ஆயிரத்து எண்கழஞ்சு ... எட்டுக்கடை நிறுத்த) with the talaikkol, and Kovalan bought her garland; in Madurai the talaikkol dancers receive the same sum (எட்டுக் கடைநிறுத்த ஆயிரத் தெண்கழஞ்சு) every day by fixed rule, and both passages praise the house as வடுநீங்கு சிறப்பின்.
links.teaches: The price that marked Madhavi's debut as a singular royal honour, and began Kovalan's ruin, turns out in Madurai to be the standing daily fee of a whole profession, and Kovalan walks past it as a man who has already paid it.

links.note: The couplet says those whose knowledge is refined by good sense do not sink into the common charms of women who are everyone's; the epic says that in the net of the dancers' glances even ascetics' hard-won wisdom turns to something else.
links.teaches: The Kural makes refined knowledge a protection against the courtesan, and the epic's street denies the guarantee by naming ascetics among those caught, so the pair shows the rule holding only for the wise who stay away, not for any wisdom that walks into the street.

gains.a: the epic's hyperbole gains its edge from the rule it breaks: the ascetic's fall matters because wisdom was supposed to protect
gains.b: the couplet gains a limit: its protection is a claim about who abstains, and the epic shows a learned art that even the disciplined are said to fall before

links.note: The Maduraikkanchi's courtesans of Madurai drain the wealth of rich young men and leave them like bees leaving a spent flower; the epic's courtesans of the same city are masters of the two styles of dance and its treatises, paid a fixed fee by rule, before whom kings bow.
links.teaches: The Sangam poem sees Madurai's courtesans as the drain on the young rich, while the epic sees them as an institution of learned art with a royal tariff, so the pair shows the epic recasting a city's vice as its high culture, the very shift that made Madhavi's art and Kovalan's ruin the same thing.

gains.a: the epic's dancers' quarter gains its older picture, in which the same women of the same city appear as takers of wealth, which the epic's praise silently suppresses
gains.b: the Sangam poem's courtesans gain an account of their art and its rules, which the poem, seeing them only from the side of the spent lover, does not give

links.note: Madurai's gem street is full of men who tell gems apart by the flaws the treatises name; before the king Kannaki says her anklet holds gems, the queen's holds pearls, and when she breaks it a gem flies to the king's mouth and he declares himself the thief.
links.teaches: The city Kovalan admires is one where every stone is judged by rule, yet the king condemns him on a goldsmith's word without testing the anklet, and the truth comes only when Kannaki breaks it, so the pairing shows the failure was not of the city's knowledge but of the king's will to use it.

links.note: The Maduraikkanchi lists in Madurai's four streets (நால்வேறு தெருவினும்) the shell-cutters, gem-borers, goldsmiths, gold-assayers and cloth-sellers; the epic closes its tour with the gold-assayers, cloth street, grain street and the four streets (நால்வேறு தெருவும்).
links.teaches: The epic follows the Sangam catalogue of Madurai's trades down to the four streets, but where the Sangam poem lists them as the plenty of a victorious Pandya, the epic shows them through a stranger about to be condemned by one of these trades, so the inherited praise of the city becomes the setting of its fall.

gains.a: the epic's tour gains a source and a measure: it is the classic praise of Madurai, which makes its turn toward ruin a turn against a known tradition
gains.b: the Sangam catalogue gains a later reading in which the gold-assayers it lists among the city's glories include the trade that will bring about the city's burning

source_issues: The kaathai header gives 218 lines but the printed last line number is 215; the edition's line numbering and the file's sequence differ by three lines somewhere in the kaathai, and line numbers here follow the file.
Line 6 reads ஒங்குயர் where ஓங்குயர் is expected, likely a lost long vowel mark.
Lines 188 and 190 carry the tool's repair of ௌ before a vowel sign to ெள (தெளித்தனைய); the repaired forms read correctly.
